tweet.text:
vLLM was the starting line. Real LLM serving begins now.

Making one model fast on one GPU is a solved problem. PagedAttention, continuous batching and good kernels got us there.

Production is different. You run dozens of replicas, and round-robin load balancing is wrong for them. Each replica holds its own KV cache, requests vary wildly in cost, and a long prompt can occupy a GPU for seconds.

The serving stack is now being built around the engine, in layers:

Client sends an OpenAI-style request.
Envoy, as a Kubernetes Gateway API gateway, receives it. It’s the data plane, and it does the proxying, TLS and streaming.
Envoy calls the Gateway API Inference Extension’s Endpoint Picker over ext_proc. The picker checks live metrics from every pod (queue depth, KV cache usage, prefix cache hits, loaded adapters) and returns the best endpoint.
Envoy forwards the request straight to that pod in the InferencePool.
llm-d runs the pool. Its scheduler logic is the brain behind the picker, and it adds prefill/decode disaggregation and KV cache aware routing on top of vLLM.
vLLM does what it does best, and tokens stream back along the same path.

Each layer has one job:
→ Envoy moves bytes.
→ The Endpoint Picker decides where each request goes.
→ llm-d turns a pile of vLLM pods into one serving system.
→ vLLM turns GPUs into tokens.
The engine is no longer the whole story. Routing, cache locality and scheduling now decide your latency and cost.

#LLM #Kubernetes #vLLM #MLOps #AIInfrastructure #Envoy
